summary:
The week was dominated by a sharp escalation and de-escalation in the Iran-U.S. conflict. On July 27, President Trump paused planned strikes on Iran as officials weighed dwindling air defense stocks. Two days later, Iran launched a missile attack on U.S. forces, prompting U.S.-Saudi strikes in Iraq on July 29. The U.S. then carried out heavy strikes on Iran on July 30. By August 2, Trump cancelled further strikes amid reports of progress on a deal. Talks advanced earlier in the week when Iran and Oman sought a Hormuz Strait agreement to jumpstart peace negotiations. Also on July 28, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Zelensky each met Trump at the White House for the first time since the Iran war began, signaling thawing relations.

Natural disasters also shaped the week. A magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck Japan's Kyushu on July 28, triggering a tsunami warning. The death toll rose from 13 on July 29 to 34 by July 30 as rescuers raced to find survivors trapped in a collapsed mall. In China, flash floods killed dozens in Gansu on August 2, with landslides feared as rain continued.

The migrant crisis in Europe flared on August 2, when 50,000 migrants surged into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, leaving dozens dead. Meanwhile, Russia's war on Ukraine continued with an overnight barrage on Kyiv that killed nine, exposing a persistent air defense gap.

Several stories emerged but faded quickly. Wildfires that forced mass evacuations in France and Spain and threatened defense sites near Bordeaux appeared only on July 27. A shooting at a Seattle food festival that killed three and injured several on the same day also did not persist. Economic stories—China's chipmaking profits surging 2,579% in the first half and Hong Kong exports soaring 53% to a record $81.7 billion in June—were widely noted on July 28 but dropped from coverage afterward.

Overall, the Iran-U.S. confrontation, the Kyushu earthquake, and the Ceuta migrant surge remained the most consequential and lasting stories, while the others proved to be one-day developments.
